opus-5.5.text:
I think the range is enormous, and honestly we're only at the very beginning of it. If you look at where AI has had its big successes so far, it's largely been in language and images, domains where there's a huge amount of data on the internet and where the "ground truth" is ultimately what humans say or see. But the physical world is different. It's governed by physical laws, it spans many scales, from quantum chemistry all the way up to weather and climate, and in most of these areas we simply don't have internet-scale data. So you can't just take a language model and expect it to understand fluid dynamics or materials behavior.

That's why so much of my work has focused on things like neural operators. The idea is that instead of learning a mapping between fixed-size vectors, you learn mappings between functions, which is what physical phenomena really are. A fluid flow, a stress field in a material, the electromagnetic field around a device: these are continuous objects. If your model can work at any resolution and respect the underlying physics, you can train on a mix of coarse simulations, fine simulations, and real experimental data, and then generalize in a way standard deep learning can't.

Once you have that, the applications open up everywhere. Weather forecasting is a great example. With FourCastNet we showed you could get forecasts tens of thousands of times faster than traditional numerical weather prediction while staying competitive in accuracy. That changes what's possible: you can run huge ensembles and get much better estimates of extreme events. The same applies to carbon capture and storage, where you want to model how CO2 moves underground over decades, or to fusion, where you need to predict plasma behavior quickly enough to control it.

Then there's design, which I'm especially excited about. Instead of only simulating, you can use these models to design things: better airfoils, medical devices, chip components, drones. We've done work on designing a catheter that reduces bacterial contamination, where the AI model helped find a geometry humans wouldn't have intuited, and it was then validated experimentally. That loop of AI proposing designs, physics-aware models evaluating them quickly, and experiments confirming them is extremely powerful.

And it extends into biology and chemistry too: protein design, drug discovery, new materials for batteries and catalysts. These are fundamentally physical problems at the molecular level.

So my view is that the next frontier of AI isn't just better chatbots. It's AI that truly understands the physical world, and can help us simulate, design, and discover things that would take decades with traditional methods. That's where I think the most transformative impact on science and engineering will come from.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the range is enormous, and honestly we've only scratched the surface. When people think about AI for the physical world, they often think about robotics, but I'd actually start somewhere much broader, which is anything governed by the laws of physics that we currently simulate with numerical solvers. That's weather and climate, fluid dynamics, materials, molecular interactions, structural engineering, even nuclear fusion. All of those are described by partial differential equations, and for decades the only way to solve them was to discretize space and time on a grid and crunch through it on a supercomputer.

What changed for me was realizing that you can learn the solution operator itself rather than learning a function on a fixed grid. That's the idea behind neural operators. Once you learn the mapping from, say, initial conditions to the evolved state, you're resolution-independent, and you can get speedups of tens of thousands of times over traditional solvers. That isn't just an efficiency gain. It changes what questions you can ask. For weather, FourCastNet lets you run thousands of ensemble members instead of a handful, so you can actually quantify uncertainty about an extreme event rather than just produce one forecast. For carbon capture, you can simulate where the CO2 plume goes underground fast enough to actually optimize injection sites instead of picking one and hoping.

Then there's the inverse direction, which I find even more exciting. Design problems. If you can evaluate a candidate quickly and differentiate through the model, you can search over designs. We've done this with medical catheters, where the model found a geometry that dramatically reduces bacterial contamination, and the physical prototype matched. We've done it with aircraft components and with plasma shapes in tokamaks. That loop of simulate, optimize, fabricate, validate is where I think AI stops being a prediction tool and becomes a discovery tool.

Now, the honest caveats. Physical data is expensive and scarce compared to text. You don't get a trillion tokens of turbulence. So the inductive biases matter a lot more, you have to bake in conservation laws, symmetries, multi-scale structure, and you need to be rigorous about where the model is extrapolating versus interpolating. Extreme events are precisely the cases you have the least data for, and they're the ones that matter most. That's why I don't see this as replacing physics. It's a partnership where the physics constrains the learning and the learning accelerates the physics.

And the last piece is closing the loop with the real world, which brings you back to robotics and autonomous labs. Once your models are fast and reasonably faithful, you can let an agent propose an experiment, run it, observe the result, and update. That's where I think the next few years get really interesting, because the bottleneck shifts from compute to how well we can make the physical world legible to these systems.

astra-6.text:
I see a very broad range, because so many physical-world problems involve understanding how a system evolves and then asking how we can change it. That could be weather and climate, fluid flows around an aircraft, or the behavior of a new material. The underlying physics differs, but there is a common need to model complex interactions across scales.

And it’s not just about predicting what happens next. It’s also about design: Can we find a shape, a material, or an operating condition that gives us the behavior we want? Traditional simulations can be expensive, which limits how many possibilities we can explore. AI can help accelerate that exploration.

The key is to bring physics and data together. We have physical laws, numerical simulations, and observations, and we should use all of them. Then we need to understand where a model is reliable and where it needs more information. That’s what makes these methods useful for real scientific and engineering problems.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the range is incredibly broad. Whenever you have a physical process—fluid flow, heat transfer, interactions between materials—you have an opportunity to build AI models that help you understand and predict it. That spans weather and climate, designing better aircraft, developing new materials, and modeling medical devices or biological systems.

What’s exciting is that we can move beyond predicting what happens to asking, “How do we design something with the properties we want?” If you can simulate a physical system much faster, you can explore many more designs and optimize them.

But the physical world also brings constraints. You need to respect the underlying physics, handle different scales, and understand where the model is reliable. So I see AI working together with scientific knowledge and numerical simulation to make these problems more tractable.
